segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: From WBEZ Chicago, it's This American Life. I'm David Kestenbaum, sitting in for Ira Glass.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: This morning on the subway, this guy brought his own chair.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: [LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: I was sitting next to him, but he was in a foldout chair.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: That's Aviva DeKornfeld, apparently our transportation correspondent. She came in to the studio to tell me a story about a woman on a bus ride that went very strangely.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: Her name's Duck. Or that's her nickname. That's what we're going to call her. She takes this bus between New York and DC a lot, back and forth. So on this trip, she's going from New York to DC, Union Station. And she's leaving around 6:00 PM at night. And she has this whole routine around the bus because she's done this trip a million times. This is Duck.

segments.speaker: Duck
segments.text: Then I'll go get a margarita, get on the bus, take a nap, wake up back home in DC. I boarded the bus as normal. They checked me in. The guy had the app with all the passengers. He made a little announcement. And they even-- I remember distinctly, they said, there's no stops planned. Great.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: Are you good at sleeping on public transit?

segments.speaker: Duck
segments.text: I can pretty much sleep anywhere.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: Oh my god, you're so lucky.

segments.speaker: Duck
segments.text: My parents would always joke that I could sleep through anything.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: So she goes to sleep. And then she wakes up around 9:00 PM to a bunch of commotion. And all the passengers are talking on the bus about what's going on. And what's going on is really odd, and so odd that Duck starts writing a thread about this online, which is how I heard about it. Here's the first post she writes.

segments.speaker: Duck
segments.text: I just woke up from a nap, and somehow, while I was asleep, everyone on the bus has figured out that we are not going to the right place.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Aviva, do they think there's a mistake or something?

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: Well, the driver of the bus is apparently telling passengers, like, I'm not going to the wrong place. You're on the wrong bus. This bus isn't going to Washington, DC. It's going further south to Virginia. And we're not going to stop. So Duck writes another post.

segments.speaker: Duck
segments.text: He's refusing to talk to anyone while he's driving and is now driving really fast. I think this is when the attitude on the bus starts to turn a little bit towards maybe we're not in a safe situation.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: And what do they think is going on? Like, is it possible they just got on the wrong bus?

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: No, because every person on the bus has been checked in by the driver as going to Washington, DC.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: And all their tickets say to DC.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: So this is the situation. They're all basically trapped on a bus. And the driver is not doing what bus drivers have typically done in the history of bus driving. I'm not sure exactly how to say this, but, whatever you think of President Trump, maybe this is a feeling you have been experiencing? He's made hundreds of millions of dollars selling meme coins to his fans and other people. He is bombing boats off Venezuela. He's tearing down the East Wing and building a giant ballroom.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Maybe this makes you feel like everything's out of control. Or maybe you're fine with it. Maybe the bus driver is a genius, and you think we should all just sit back and see. In this case, though, the passengers are not into it. And when a person has so completely left the normal script of things, the question is, what do you do?

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: So the first thing they try to do is reason with the bus driver, reassert the normal facts and rules for the bus ride. Duck said that two guys went up to him at the front of the bus and said, man to man, we're going to Union Station.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: And?

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: He said, no, we're not. Didn't work.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: What do they try next?

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: After that, someone notices that he has a French accent and thinks, oh, maybe this is a language barrier issue. So they start talking to him in French and then end up arguing with him in French. And then it becomes very clear it is not a language barrier issue.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Wow.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: And then Duck just starts firing off post after post. And you can feel things escalating as you're reading the thread. And it's like, first, the bus company is trying to call the driver, and he's not answering. And then someone pulls up Waze and sees that they're going 20 miles over the speed limit. And then someone gets the bus company on speakerphone and is walking it up to the front of the bus. And then Duck could actually hear the bus company guy yelling, you're going to Union Station, to the bus driver. And then he screams in response that he doesn't get paid enough and is refusing.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Wow.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: And then person after person-- each kind of feels like they're going to be the hero who convinces the bus driver to get back on track. And so each person takes their phone with the company reps on speakerphone to the bus driver. And then in response, he just grabs them and hangs up.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Why don't they call the police?

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: Well, so then that is the next thing that people are thinking about doing. So while a couple passengers are in the front of the bus, fighting with the driver, the rest of the people in the back of the bus are debating whether or not to call the police. Because half the bus is thinking this is actually just going to agitate him further, and that feels dangerous. And the other half are like, well, the bus company can't help us. So who is the next authority figure who can come to our help?

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: So what happens?

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: Eventually, someone does call the police. And Duck's next post is, quote, "OK. Someone called the police but suggested they avoid pulling over the bus because he's driving so erratically. We are passing DC."

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: So they feel like they're in danger?

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: The bus is kind of split. Half the bus feels like they're in the sequel to the movie Speed.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Like they're being kidnapped or something.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: Yes. And then the other half feels like, you know what? Let's just sit tight, see what happens.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: In the dark at, like, 75 miles an hour on some highway.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: Yes.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: It's like they tried all these things, and now there's nothing else they can do.

segments.speaker: Duck
segments.text: There's a good bit of wanting the situation to be otherwise and wanting it to be easily figureoutable in the moment and not having to wait for something bad to happen or wait to figure out how it all resolves.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: Yeah. And then at some point, you're like, well, I guess we just have to-- it's actually up to him.

segments.speaker: Duck
segments.text: We have to go on this entire bus ride, no matter where it ends.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: So he does eventually get off the highway in Vienna, Virginia.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Like he promised.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: And he does, weirdly, sort of go through the normal motions of a bus driver at a bus stop. And he helps everyone get off and get their luggage from underneath the bus, and-- although people are yelling at him, and he's kind of yelling back. And he's flipping people off. And then once everyone's off, he just drives off.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Did they ever get an answer to what was going on with the guy?

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: No. But the bus company did send another bus to Virginia to pick them up and take them back to DC. And that bus driver was very apologetic and was like, sorry about that other guy. I think he's new.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: I think he's new?

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: Yes, which does not seem like the behavior of a new bus driver to me. But--

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: But they made it home?

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: Yes. They made it home.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: We did reach out to the bus company. A spokesperson said the driver does not work there anymore. He had disobeyed his supervisor's instructions. Quote, "As to what caused him to do so, we are not sure."

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: Duck said that the bus ride from Vienna, Virginia, back to DC, their original destination, was very quiet.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Today on the show, people who find themselves on journeys they did not intend or agree to. They find themselves trapped on these journeys, and they have to figure out what to do. In one story, a famous tree disappears from a landscape overnight. Also, one woman's shockingly difficult quest to get some badly needed-ice cubes. Stay with us.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: It's This American Life. Act One, The Gardener. Sometimes the bus ride you're stuck on, against your will, is the thoughts that are spinning around in your own mind. Ayman Oghanna has a story like that. He's a reporter who's been on our show before, does his stories from a lot of different countries and conflict zones. Here he is.

segments.speaker: Ayman Oghanna
segments.text: My wife and I live in a sleepy seaside town on the outskirts of Athens, the kind of place where nothing interesting ever happens. She says that's why we live there. We run into our neighbors all the time in our small apartment building. Below us, two floors down, is this guy, Christos. He's a Greek air force colonel in his mid 50s, has a family-- a traditional kind of guy.

segments.speaker: Klea
segments.text: He has this kind of clean face, bright eyes, always a little bit shy and ready to help.

segments.speaker: Ayman Oghanna
segments.text: This is my wife, Klea.

segments.speaker: Klea
segments.text: Like, he will always be helpful with door or with the cat, Kuku.

segments.speaker: Ayman Oghanna
segments.text: Kuku is our cat. He's an indoor-outdoor cat. And to be honest, he's kind of an asshole, bites me in my sleep sometimes. But Christos is always nice to him.

segments.speaker: Klea
segments.text: So he would always be gentle with Kuku, open the door to Kuku, and say, hey, how are you? Even talk to my cat-- this is what I want to say. So the feeling I have is just this kind, trusted person in our building.

segments.speaker: Ayman Oghanna
segments.text: Christos shares the apartment with his wife, teenage daughter, and mother-in-law. The wife and mother-in-law, in our experience, are not so nice, the opposite of Christos, always yelling at him, causing problems in the building. When we heard Christos's family yelling at him, it always felt a bit sad. He never shouted back, never defended himself. He just absorbed it quietly.

segments.speaker: Ayman Oghanna
segments.text: In the evenings, he'd water the small vegetable patch in front of our building-- tomatoes, cabbages, peppers pushing up through dry soil. He was the most ordinary presence imaginable, until one day in February.

segments.speaker: Klea
segments.text: I'll tell you how I find out about this. So I was with my mum, Chloe. And Pardis and everyone was there.

segments.speaker: Ayman Oghanna
segments.text: Your family.

segments.speaker: Klea
segments.text: My family. So my family was there. And out of the blue, my mum says, did you find out about Christos? Did you heard what happened in the news? And I'm totally confused. I didn't know what she was talking about. And then she explains, Christos that lives in the building, he was caught by the police. He is caught by the police about what? I'm like, what? And she says, oh, yeah, he's a spy. It was like a bomb.

segments.speaker: Ayman Oghanna
segments.text: International espionage in our little apartment building. According to news reports, the Greek intelligence service had been quietly monitoring him for months. He's accused of passing classified NATO material to China, and it may take a long time to fully assess the damage.

segments.speaker: Ayman Oghanna
segments.text: For his part, Christos has largely admitted to the charges. We reached out to him and his family. Through his lawyer, Christos said he initially thought he was working with a private company on a legitimate business opportunity. He didn't know they were actually working with the Chinese government. And gradually, he was pressured into spying. He apologized to his country, the armed forces, his colleagues, and his family. Reportedly, he's cooperating with investigators.

segments.speaker: Ayman Oghanna
segments.text: But that's not really why I'm telling you this story. I'm telling it because for years, I was convinced there were spies all around me. 10 years ago, I was diagnosed with bipolar disorder. I've had episodes of paranoia, sometimes psychosis, often involving spies. And now, here we were, with an accused spy living in our building.

segments.speaker: Ayman Oghanna
segments.text: Madness doesn't arrive suddenly. It slides in quietly, like a familiar voice, whispering things you've longed to hear. My most recent episode happened a few years ago. I had just returned from a reporting trip to Israel in the occupied West Bank. It started with my phone. It seemed to be behaving strangely, overheating in my hand, apps freezing, missed calls appearing from countries I'd never been. These could all be explained, of course, if, say, I was under surveillance.

segments.speaker: Ayman Oghanna
segments.text: Then I started noticing suspicious people-- Chinese tourists taking pictures on their phones of things that weren't particularly interesting. What about that delivery bike idling too long outside the building? One afternoon, I saw a woman in sunglasses walking the same way as me, which I took as a sign I was being followed. So I hopped on an Athens city bus. I'd given her the slip, only to find myself arriving in the airport, which is a perfect place if you're imagining international espionage-- people from all over the globe, flights from Istanbul, Vienna, Doha, strange tongues, faces, and people.

segments.speaker: Ayman Oghanna
segments.text: But none stranger than me-- I wandered departures, slyly photographing people I thought were agents. I uploaded photos of them to Instagram to let them know I had them made. It was exhilarating. Mania can feel electric. When I was in this state, people would notice that I was off and presume I was drunk or high.

segments.speaker: Ayman Oghanna
segments.text: Loved ones who knew me better could see something was wrong and suggested getting help. But I wouldn't listen, convinced that they were trying to lock me up in a psych ward to silence me, preventing me from carrying out my hazy mission, like I had some purpose but didn't know what it was. Soon, I was sure there were spies in the building. Weirdly, one person I did not suspect, even in psychosis, was mild-mannered Christos.

segments.speaker: Ayman Oghanna
segments.text: Klea watched me spin out. We'd recently gotten engaged, and now I was talking about spies all the time. At first, she told herself it would pass. Then she realized it might not, which was frightening. And then I disappeared. After a few days, Klea called the British Embassy and the police. They eventually found me, detained me, and took me to a mental hospital.

segments.speaker: Klea
segments.text: Yeah. That was scary. It was scary. Because I was afraid you might never come back again in your stable place, that I would never see and talk to the person I remember. Oh, also, I remember this. In this madness, there were moments where you had your sanity. That was so, so weird.

segments.speaker: Ayman Oghanna
segments.text: Like what?

segments.speaker: Klea
segments.text: Like, I remember you were at the psychiatric hospital, right? And the nurse was trying to convince you to stay stable and have your vaccine.

segments.speaker: Ayman Oghanna
segments.text: Not vaccine-- injection.

segments.speaker: Klea
segments.text: Injection, sorry-- in order for you to calm down, because the police was there. And they would had to put handcuffs in order to transport you from the public hospital to the private one. And you were in denial. You were like, I'm not doing this. So in some point, you said, I want my fiancee to come. And that's my condition. If she comes, then I'll-- so you were negotiating things. And when they were transporting you, I was with them. And you said, my love, didn't I promise you adventures? So here you are. These are the adventures.

segments.speaker: Ayman Oghanna
segments.text: Later, she told me she'd started to wonder if I was a spy, that my obsession with espionage made more sense if I was somehow part of it. It turns out, delusions about espionage and religion are extremely common in people who have bipolar disorder. After a few weeks in hospital, I was released. Klea found a bespectacled, goateed professor of psychiatry who she hoped could help me. He introduced me to something called psychoeducation. I'd seen shrinks before but had some bad experiences.

segments.speaker: Ayman Oghanna
segments.text: Psychoeducation was different. It taught me to learn the mechanics of my disorder the way a psychiatrist would-- what triggers look like, how symptoms stacked up, what the early warning lights were. I was less a passive patient and more a junior practitioner in my own case. I started to map my own warning signs-- a broken sleep cycle, the rush of success. I made sure to always take my meds as prescribed and guard my sleep like it was my job, especially on the days that I felt least like doing either.

segments.speaker: Ayman Oghanna
segments.text: When I sat up, typing revelations at 2:00 AM, convinced I had uncovered truth, the rule was simple-- type them out, but don't send them to anyone. Then check in daylight. Most mornings, the revelation looked like nonsense from an overheated mind. For the first few months, it was hard to admit that none of it had actually happened. I went back over it all, searching for proof that it was real, that someone really was watching me. I've learned to remind myself that coincidences do happen all the time. Everything can be a symbol if you let it.

segments.speaker: Ayman Oghanna
segments.text: When Klea found out Christos had been arrested, I was in Syria on a reporting trip. She was worried how I would respond to the news.

segments.speaker: Klea
segments.text: How am I going to tell Ayman that what he was telling me is true, this kind of ironic situation? My fear was like, what if I trigger you? I trigger something bad. So that was a point when I called you. And I remember you were in Syria, reporting. And I said the whole story fast. But in every sentence, I remember you were always saying, whoa, this is unbelievable. Whoa. This is unbelievable.

segments.speaker: Ayman Oghanna
segments.text: I remember standing on the hotel balcony in Syria, the phone to my ear, taking it in and thinking not just how strange it was, but that I wasn't going loopy-- no paranoia.

segments.speaker: Klea
segments.text: The way you reacted on it was very, very-- I would say impressive-- and relief, made me feel relief. Because you got the information, you process it, and it felt like you accept it as it is, that this is reality, and your neighbor might be a spy.

segments.speaker: Ayman Oghanna
segments.text: I just remember how amazing it was. I felt like, yeah, OK, you're not completely crazy. Like, there are spies out there, and there's one in your building. And it felt almost like a part of me was like, yes.

segments.speaker: Ayman Oghanna
segments.text: [RATTLING]

segments.speaker: Klea
segments.text: That's your meds.

segments.speaker: Ayman Oghanna
segments.text: That's the reminder for my meds, which is very appropriate.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: When I got home from Syria, I was still trying to wrap my head around the news about Christos. I went to the garden where he used to carefully water the vegetable patch every evening. Now weeds had started pushing up through the rows. It was getting overgrown. No one was coming down to tend it. Christos is in jail, awaiting trial. For a long time, his boots stayed outside his door. His family are still here. In the garage, his car has gathered dust.

segments.speaker: Klea
segments.text: So I want to ask this. What was exciting, when you were psychotic, about the feeling of somebody spying on me or there are spies out there?

segments.speaker: Ayman Oghanna
segments.text: It's like a validation. You go through your life unnoticed, and you want someone to pay attention to you. And the idea that someone's watching you appeals to your ego that there's some higher power that cares about you, whether it's God or an intelligence agency.

segments.speaker: Klea
segments.text: And how do you feel about somebody that actually is a spy? Do you like him? Do you admire him? Do you dislike him?

segments.speaker: Ayman Oghanna
segments.text: Well, you're a spy, right?

segments.speaker: Klea
segments.text: I'm a spy.

segments.speaker: Klea
segments.text: [LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Klea
segments.text: Part-time job.

segments.speaker: Klea
segments.text: [LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Ayman Oghanna
segments.text: No, I don't think I admire them or that it's something I want to do. And also, I'd be terrified, having this secret from you. [LAUGHS] You would definitely find out if I was a spy.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: There really are spies, but they're not after me. They're just people living quiet, dangerous lives I'll never fully understand. I'm OK with leaving the secret missions to them.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Ayman Oghanna is a reporter in Greece.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Act Two, No Power To The People. Our show today is about people who feel like they're trapped in some situation they have no control over, like passengers on a runaway bus. And we turn next to a place where there are actually not a lot of buses running right now because the country is out of oil. It's from writer Eileen Sosin Martinez, who lives in Havana. Because it's hard to even make phone calls from there, we got an actor to read it.

segments.speaker: Actor As Eileen
segments.text: About two weeks ago, I had a silly accident. I took a step backwards, thinking the sidewalk was there, but ended up stepping onto thin air. My left knee, which underwent surgery many years ago, couldn't hold me up, and I suffered a sprain. The doctor told me to take anti-inflammatories for 10 days and apply ice every two hours. I got naproxen pills on the black market, as is usually the case, given the shortage plaguing state-run pharmacies. Finding the pills was supposed to be the hard part.

segments.speaker: Actor As Eileen
segments.text: Though obvious looking back, it didn't occur to me that the other part of my treatment, icing my knee every two hours, would be even harder to carry out. I filled up a half-liter bottle with water and put it in the freezer. Easy, right? Yes, if you have power. The power company used to publish a weekly blackout schedule. They'd never fully stick to it, but you'd at least get an idea of whether they would cut the power in the morning or afternoon. And usually, it would be out for no more than four hours.

segments.speaker: Actor As Eileen
segments.text: But at the end of 2025, the blackouts started increasing. Then, in January, the United States launched an oil embargo, threatening tariffs on any country supplying Cuba with oil. In the spring, the situation changed again for the worse. The oil we got from a Russian tanker at the end of March ran out in early May. I expected an uptick in blackouts, but I never thought it would be this bad.

segments.speaker: Actor As Eileen
segments.text: Now we don't talk about blackouts. We talk about whiteouts, [SPANISH], as they would say in the so-called "special period" of the '90s, the crisis that devastated Cuba following the collapse of the Soviet Union. In other words, instead of counting how many hours a day the power is cut, we count how long it's back on. Blackouts are the rule and power the exception.

segments.speaker: Actor As Eileen
segments.text: These whiteouts had been happening for at least a year in other provinces, but not in Havana. Now, not even favoritism can shield the capital from them. We are barely getting three hours of electricity a day, five at most. So, of course, there wasn't enough time for the ice I was supposed to be using on my knee to fully set. Instead of ice, I've been using cold water, a sort of slush. I alternate where I place the bottle-- on the underside of my knee, on the outside, on top, on bottom. I'm supposed to do this for 20 minutes.

segments.speaker: Actor As Eileen
segments.text: If I had ice, it would ease the pain almost immediately. Cold water just cools off the skin. Still, I keep a bottle in the freezer, hoping. I remember how I'd react when the blackouts first got worse at the end of last year. When the power went out, I'd be overcome with an urge to do something, anything. It was winter, and it would already be dark at 6:00 PM. So I would exercise in the dark, read by flashlight, and wash some of my clothes by hand.

segments.speaker: Actor As Eileen
segments.text: Now it's flipped. When the electricity goes out, I feel drained, helpless. But I feel euphoric when the power's back on. Are you happy, my love? My boyfriend asked me on one of these occasions. It was only then that I realized I was singing while dicing onions for dinner. When the electricity is back on, people run to their washing machines, hoping the power lasts enough to get the laundry done. That's also the only chance to use the blender to have juice for breakfast or to make puree for a baby.

segments.speaker: Actor As Eileen
segments.text: I'm lucky. I have a gas stove, but many rely on electricity to cook. They use those precious hours to turn on rice and multicookers so there'll be food for the next day. Then everyone, rich and poor alike, faces the same problem-- how to preserve food. You need a whole system and a great memory.

segments.speaker: Actor As Eileen
segments.text: The first rule is, don't cook what you planned. Cook what's defrosting the fastest. For example, if you open a can of tomato sauce or corn, you have to store it again in a plastic container and put it in the freezer. The lower part of the fridge barely works and is now basically a cupboard. Cooked rice, cooked pasta, it all goes in the freezer. I've had to throw out so much food because of lack of refrigeration-- carrots, chicken, mangoes, yucca, way too much rice. Throwing out food in the middle of food shortages feels like sacrilege.

segments.speaker: Actor As Eileen
segments.text: And while we're all going slowly mad waiting for a small cube of ice to form in the freezer, there are other indignities-- for example, the trash, which piles up on street corners like monuments to this disaster. This also isn't a new problem. For the past few years, garbage collection has varied throughout cities and neighborhoods. Maybe the truck went by yesterday in some places and weeks or months ago in others. But now, it's much worse.

segments.speaker: Actor As Eileen
segments.text: According to officials, there's no gas for garbage trucks, which, to top things off, break down with no replacement parts available. Clinging to a shred of civic responsibility, we take out our household trash and walk for a few blocks until we find bins that aren't overflowing, leaving it where it's least obstructive.

segments.speaker: Actor As Eileen
segments.text: Just a few yards from my door, you'll find one of those garbage piles, haloed by innumerable flies that have also made their way into my home. They're always riled up early in the morning, touching your arm and back and buzzing in your face while you're making coffee. I'll brush them off and shoo them away, but they come back. It doesn't matter that everything's clean. They're already inside. And you can't take your eyes off your mug or the bread you got for breakfast, because they'll land on them the minute you do.

segments.speaker: Actor As Eileen
segments.text: A few days ago, I heard a neighbor complain about the heat, but she would rather shut all her doors and windows than let in flies. Sometimes I'll also leave my windows closed to keep out the stench of garbage. I'll peek out onto the street and see flies in the flower garden landing on tall grass, bending over under their weight, as if it were a wheat stalk made up of insects instead of grains.

segments.speaker: Actor As Eileen
segments.text: People started setting these piles of garbage on fire, and there was smoke everywhere. So much garbage is still there, and the temperature's rising. I wouldn't be surprised if one day, there's a spontaneous combustion. That's a real thing that can happen. A few days ago, the garbage pile near my house caught fire. We heard a little explosion, and when I looked out the window, it had already started burning.

segments.speaker: Actor As Eileen
segments.text: I called the firefighters at 5:00 PM. It was very windy, and the smoke cloud was spreading. A while went by, and since the firemen hadn't come, my boyfriend and I took advantage of the fact that the flames had died down a bit and doused them with buckets of water. We thought we'd put them out, but that wasn't the case. I kept calling the emergency line. The firefighters finally arrived at 8:00 PM. Our house smelled like smoke for days.

segments.speaker: Actor As Eileen
segments.text: I don't know what's more disturbing, the growing number of sleepless nights or the torture of not knowing how much longer this will last. I still haven't found an answer to the latter. To try and solve the former, the restless nights, we bought a rechargeable fan-- $40 for a tiny plastic fan. My fan pretty much looks like a toy, but now I no longer wake up sweating in the middle of the night.

segments.speaker: Actor As Eileen
segments.text: The sound of the spinning blades has become a sort of lullaby that helps me fall asleep, like so many people on this sweltering island, because on blackout nights, sometimes the silence is more frightening than the darkness. I live at the end of an avenue where you used to hear loud conversations, music, and cars well past midnight. Now, the streets are empty.

segments.speaker: Actor As Eileen
segments.text: I don't exactly sleep like a baby. If the power comes back at 2:00 or 4:00 in the morning, I have to leap out of bed and charge everything-- power banks, the lamp, the laptop. And if they shut it off before morning, I have to get up again and turn the rechargeable fan back on. Lately, whenever my mom or aunts message me on WhatsApp to ask me how I'm doing, I almost always answer, "I'm here, in a blackout," as if I too only ran on electricity, as if the darkness and silence were a part of me.

segments.speaker: Actor As Eileen
segments.text: A few nights ago, a bunch of neighbors started banging on pots and pans. I've seen countless videos on social media of these cacerolazos. But I'd never had it happen so close, on my own block. Honestly, it sounded more like a raging party than public outcry. You could hear voices yelling, vamos! And bang them, bang them! It felt like a kind of release, like their weariness had reached its limit. And at the same time, there was a sense of fun, of mischief. Aside from two or three notable occasions, there hasn't been a massive protest in Cuba in decades. But now we have these cacerolazos.

segments.speaker: Actor As Eileen
segments.text: After about 15 minutes of outrage, the power came back on. It was probably just a coincidence, but it felt wonderful to hear shouts of joy, as if the protests had really worked. And then a few minutes after that, the power shut back off. Nobody yelled or made any noise.

segments.speaker: Actor As Eileen
segments.text: A few days later, they turned the power back on at night, and it lasted until 6:00 in the morning. These were seven hours where the fridge door was barely opened, which meant that the next morning, my half-liter water bottle had completely frozen. 10 days after getting my doctor's orders, I was finally able to ice my left knee.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Actor Ana Villafane reading a story by Eileen Sosin Martinez, whose reporting you can find in The Guardian and elsewhere. Ana is currently starring in Sinatra on London's West End. Gabriela Munoz Ravello translated Eileen's story from Spanish to English. Coming up, if a tree falls in a forest, could it ever possibly be murder? A crime that captivated England goes before a High Court judge. That's in a minute from Chicago Public Radio when our program continues.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: It's This American Life. I'm David Kestenbaum. This week's show, Trapped on a Bus, people stuck in situations they cannot control and do not like. We are at Act Three. Act Three, Murder, Tree Wrote. Sometimes an entire country can be taken on an unexpected journey against its will. That happened in England recently. And I'm not talking about their inability to keep a prime minister. I'm talking about a crime so confounding, so nonsensical, people just could not wrap their heads around it. Rosa Lyster tells the story.

segments.speaker: Rosa Lyster
segments.text: In September 2023, a farmer called the Northumberland National Park to report a fallen tree, not just any tree-- a sycamore, more than 100 years old, by some reports, the most photographed tree in Britain. It stood in the depression between two hills in the desolate landscape of the park in a gap in a stone wall. Not just any stone wall-- an especially picturesque section of Hadrian's Wall, which was built by the Romans across the narrowest part of England. Photographers went crazy for the tree.

segments.speaker: Rosa Lyster
segments.text: The park ranger who arrived at the scene assumed at first that it had been blown down by the high winds the night before, until he saw the cleanness of the cut. He told the BBC, "Once you realize it's been chopped down, then it's going to become a massive worldwide story." I'd never heard of the tree before it got cut down, and neither had anyone I knew. I live in London, though. The tree was a beloved landmark of England's North East, its silhouette instantly recognizable to those who knew it. And, as virtually every news report would go on to stress, it had also been featured in the 1991 movie, Robin Hood, Prince of Thieves.

segments.speaker: Rosa Lyster
segments.text: Even so, I was surprised to see that quite quickly, the lamentation went beyond those with a personal link to the tree. People across the country began to speak of the death of the tree, calling it slaughter and comparing its loss to that of a close family member or to the death of Princess Diana. They said they felt as if their hearts had been ripped out. They spoke of evil and desecration and named the fantastical medieval-seeming punishments that they would like to see visited on the scumbags who could have done this.

segments.speaker: Rosa Lyster
segments.text: Steve Blair, the manager of a nearby pub, told me about the day he truly understood that it was gone. It was the first snowfall, he said. You'd get people taking photographs of the tree because it's covered in snow and it looks so, so, so good. I was driving to work, and as I came over the hill, you would normally see the photographers all over Sycamore Gap. And then, on this specific day, there was no one there anymore.

segments.speaker: Rosa Lyster
segments.text: For about a month, nobody had any idea who had felled the tree. Then, acting on a tip, the Northumbria police brought in two local men, a mechanic named Adam Carruthers and his friend, a tree surgeon named Daniel Graham. Six months later, the two men appeared at Newcastle Magistrates' Court. They walked in together, a united front, wearing balaclavas to avoid the cameras outside the courthouse.

segments.speaker: Rosa Lyster
segments.text: The two men were charged with criminal damage amounting to 623,335 pounds, over 800,000 American dollars. According to prosecutors, this extraordinarily specific figure was arrived at, in part, using something called the Capital Asset Value for Amenity Trees system, a method local governments use to calculate the worth of trees. Graham pleaded not guilty, while Carruthers entered no plea.

segments.speaker: Rosa Lyster
segments.text: In the intense media coverage that followed, reporters and commentators struggled to come up with plausible reasons why the two men-- or, indeed, anyone on Earth-- would have felled the tree. Some sort of ancient act of revenge, or a grievance against the local government, possibly? Was it a protest, perhaps, driven by very left-wing ideas, or else, very right-wing ones? A case could be made for either. The explanation, whatever the hell it might be, would surely emerge at trial.

segments.speaker: Rosa Lyster
segments.text: The Sycamore Gap trial began in late April of last year. There was Carruthers, the young family man, dressed in a shiny black suit that was too big for him, blinking and swallowing and staring hard into the middle distance. And there was Graham, gaunt and guarded and fizzing with tension. He was only a few years older than Carruthers but looked old enough to be his dad.

segments.speaker: Rosa Lyster
segments.text: A senior High Court judge, Justice Christina Lambert, had been appointed. High Court judges deal with the most serious and complicated trials in England and Wales. Many of Lambert's recent cases have involved grave crimes of the sort that society considers unthinkable. In 2024, she was one of three senior judges appointed to consider the appeal of Lucy Letby, the nurse convicted of the murder of seven babies. Even at the start of the trial, there was talk of a prison sentence if the two men were found guilty.

segments.speaker: Rosa Lyster
segments.text: The atmosphere in the courtroom was notably strange, both entirely serious and entirely ridiculous. On the press bench, reporters murmured to one another that it felt a bit like a murder trial. It didn't, though, not exactly. Nobody was dead. There were no grieving family members. I couldn't seem to keep a handle on what was at stake, what law the two men had actually broken. Between sessions, I kept having to look up the legal definition of murder to check one more time whether the term could be applied to anything other than the killing of a human being. It cannot.

segments.speaker: Rosa Lyster
segments.text: At other times, people in the public gallery would burst into laughter, to Judge Lambert's immense and theatrical disapproval. She had a way of peering over her spectacles. Officially, the jury was being presented with a straightforward question of criminal damage. Were Adam Carruthers and Daniel Graham responsible for cutting down a sycamore by Hadrian's Wall on the night of September 27, 2023? Unfortunately for the defendants, this turned out to be exceptionally easy to answer.

segments.speaker: Rosa Lyster
segments.text: To begin with, there was CCTV footage of the Range Rover driving to and from the parking lot near the tree. Graham's phone was tracked traveling to and from the site. On the same phone, the police recovered a nearly three-minute video, very dimly lit, of a small figure working at the trunk of a large tree, a chainsaw droning in the background, leaning his whole weight into the job until the crackling collapse began. They also recovered a photo of a tree wedge and a chainsaw in Graham's trunk.

segments.speaker: Rosa Lyster
segments.text: The two men had sent each other voice notes, talking about the heaviness of the chainsaw and the amount of coverage that the crime was getting. In one of them, Graham seemed as if he would combust with elation, letting Carruthers know that the tree was "on fucking Sky News as we speak." What else? There was a selfie Graham had taken, in which he is squinting into the camera, looking pleased, while in the background, Carruthers once again saws away with evident expertise at the trunk of a large tree.

segments.speaker: Rosa Lyster
segments.text: Neither of the men held up well under questioning. It's strange to see people tell such brazen and low-effort lies in front of the international media and a High Court judge. Carruthers, the younger man, was by far the more amiable of the two, striving to seem tractable and reasonable while nevertheless lying flamboyantly. His approach throughout the trial was to state over and over that he had no idea who could have done it, none at all. He brought up his partner, Amy, and their two young children often. Carruthers seemed basically ordinary. He looked scared.

segments.speaker: Rosa Lyster
segments.text: Graham was different, a character from another moral universe altogether. I don't know if I've ever seen a person radiate scorn more thoroughly than he did. He seemed contemptuous of everything-- trees, other people, the concept of truth. He made a point of mentioning how alone he was in the world and how fine he was with this state of affairs. The press box is directly behind the witness stand, so I couldn't see his face as he spoke. But he still managed to make the back of his skinny, tattooed neck convey the suggestion that we all go and fuck ourselves.

segments.speaker: Rosa Lyster
segments.text: He lied beyond the point of sense or even reason, conceding that, yes, that was his car at the site, and yes, the video of the tree being sawed down was on his phone, but that none of this proved a thing. He said he left his keys in his car for the use of anyone who happened to be passing by. Carruthers could have taken it. In a police interview, Graham had provided other possibilities-- a stranger from nearby Carlisle or his stepdaughter's boyfriend. As far as I'm aware, he doesn't have a stepdaughter. He said he had "no interest" in sycamores-- "I cut trees down. I don't collect them."

segments.speaker: Rosa Lyster
segments.text: Not everything Graham said came across as a fabrication that could be dismantled on the spot. He appeared sincere, for instance, when talking about his father's suicide and about how he and Carruthers had become friends. Carruthers had helped him fix his father's Land Rover in time for the funeral. He also didn't seem to be lying, exactly, when it came to the matter of the string.

segments.speaker: Rosa Lyster
segments.text: Under questioning, he explained that he had first heard of the sycamore sometime in 2021, when he had gone into Carruthers's workshop and asked if he could borrow a piece of string. Carruthers refused, saying that the string had great sentimental meaning for him. Then, according to Graham, Carruthers laid the string in a circle on the floor of his workshop. He told Graham that the circumference of the circle exactly matched the trunk of the most famous tree in the world.

segments.speaker: Rosa Lyster
segments.text: Nobody could quite work out what to do with this story. Lawyers for both sides kept bringing it up, but no one seemed clear on how the information ought to be used. It was too weird a detail to be helpful in a courtroom, but it was also too weird to ignore, because it didn't seem like something that a person would just invent. If he'd simply wanted to account for how he had learned of the tree's existence, Graham could have said almost anything, instead of this otherworldly business about a piece of string that contains within it the essence of a beloved tree, like something out of the Brothers Grimm. In fact, the whole thing seemed like a fairytale that had made its way into a courtroom.

segments.speaker: Rosa Lyster
segments.text: It often felt as if the most important question in the courtroom was not whether Carruthers and Graham had done it, but whether they-- or anyone-- understood what it was that they had done. There was a kind of collective effort to affirm that something terrible had happened, something much worse than ordinary criminal damage, much worse than simply cutting down a tree. How else to account for the ferocity of the public indignation? At one point, Carruthers said that he hadn't been able to understand what all the fuss was about. My understanding, he said, was that it was just a tree.

segments.speaker: Rosa Lyster
segments.text: The truth is that people in Britain don't really like sycamores. Gardeners go so far as to despise them. They are among the only trees in the country that are regularly referred to as weeds. They are prolific self-seeders. One mature tree can be the parent of thousands of seedlings in a single year. They can grow almost anywhere. And they do. They are non-native, which some people have strong feelings about. The sycamore's tendency to flourish in places where plenty of other trees would wither and die might have been the reason that John Clayton, a 19th-century landowner, planted one in a gap along Hadrian's Wall.

segments.speaker: Rosa Lyster
segments.text: The wall, whose construction began in the year 122, was built to mark the northwestern boundary of the Roman Empire, serving as a frontier, customs post, and reminder of the reach of power. Clayton planted the sycamore presumably because he thought it would look nice there, an isolated tree right in the middle of a dramatic dip in the landscape, the wall running steeply up each side of it, such that hikers could look down on it as they approached.

segments.speaker: Rosa Lyster
segments.text: Carruthers and Graham were sentenced in July. Before the sentencing, a junior counsel presented a victim impact statement. This consisted of emails and messages from members of the public, read in a loud, slow, tragic voice. She tried her best. They said things like, "I've never felt this way about any other tree," and "This feels like losing a close family member," and "RIP BEAUTIFUL TREE I WISH I'D GOT TO MEET YOU."

segments.speaker: Rosa Lyster
segments.text: Carruthers and Graham were each given four years and three months in prison. The sentence seemed weirdly over the top. When people cut down a tree in England, what usually happens is nothing-- that, or a fine. The sentence, Judge Lambert said, was based on a consideration of "the social impact of the offense." People had loved the tree, she said, and Carruthers and Graham had destroyed it in an act of vandalism that was somehow both mindless and premeditated. According to a tree lawyer I talked to, it was the first time anyone in the United Kingdom had gone to prison for cutting down a single tree.

segments.speaker: Rosa Lyster
segments.text: I only got to see the stump. I visited in late spring. It was very sunny. The remnants of the sycamore come into view as you get to the top of a slithery flight of stairs set into the bank. Then you look down at the stump, which is in precisely the spot where it would have been good to come across a tree, a nice, tall one with spreading branches, pretty old, standing totally alone in the landscape, looking like the idea of shelter.

segments.speaker: Rosa Lyster
segments.text: Before this, I hadn't grasped why the locals had gotten so worked up over a single tree, let alone the rest of the country. Up close, though, their reactions made more sense. The tree had been special. And Carruthers and Graham never explained-- in a satisfying way-- why they had cut it down.

segments.speaker: Rosa Lyster
segments.text: Before their sentencing, they finally admitted they had done it. Carruthers said he was blackout drunk, and Graham said he was just keeping Carruthers company. The judge did not accept this explanation, and neither did anyone else. Whenever I talk to people about the trial, the explanation was pretty simple in their minds-- Adam Carruthers and Daniel Graham were morons. They always said that-- "morons," or else "mindless," or else "absolutely mindless and brain dead, no?"

segments.speaker: Rosa Lyster
segments.text: Almost everybody said something along these lines. They wanted to believe that Carruthers and Graham had done it because they were very stupid or not thinking at all. I could understand why. The alternative and obvious explanation-- that they had thought about it quite extensively, that they knew how much people had loved the tree and had cut it down for precisely that reason-- that's much more disturbing.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Rosa Lyster lives in London. A version of this story was first published in Harper's Magazine. Will Stephenson edited that version of the story. Aviva DeKornfeld produced our radio version.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Act Four, In Flight Snack. We started today's show with someone trapped on a bus, and we're going to end it with someone trapped on a plane. The someone is Leticia Lima. When she was 16, she was boarding a flight from Sao Paulo, where she lived, to Germany, when this older woman sat down next to her and did something that Leticia still thinks about to this day. Producer Tobin Low talked to her about that strange interaction, which started as soon as she got on the plane.

segments.speaker: Leticia Lima
segments.text: I board early. I'm sitting in my seat, which was a window seat all the way in the back of the airplane, close to the toilets in the back of the airplane. And eventually, this lady comes and sits next to me. And she immediately starts talking to me. And I thought, oh god, no. Like I've sat next to--

segments.speaker: Tobin Low
segments.text: A nightmare.

segments.speaker: Leticia Lima
segments.text: Yeah. I've sat next to someone who wants to chat. I really don't want to chat. But my parents taught me to be polite to my elders. So I'm kind of nodding along to what she's saying and trying not to engage or show too much interest but also not be rude.

segments.speaker: Tobin Low
segments.text: Yeah. What is she saying to you when she sits down?

segments.speaker: Leticia Lima
segments.text: First, she's got this bag with her, and she's taking all these things out of her bag and looking for something. And she kept apologizing that she was looking for something. And then she pulled out this huge rosary. And she's like, OK, now I've got it. And then she starts telling me, I'm quite nervous because this is my first time on an airplane.

segments.speaker: Tobin Low
segments.text: Oh, no.

segments.speaker: Leticia Lima
segments.text: And I said, oh, OK. And she said, yeah, she was from somewhere in the countryside and had taken a bus for 18 hours or something to get to Sao Paulo to fly out. And she was flying out because her daughter had gone to Germany for work and had met a German man and was getting married, and so they had sent her the tickets to come to the wedding.

segments.speaker: Leticia Lima
segments.text: But she's going on and on. And I could tell she was quite nervous because she kept fidgeting with the rosary, and she's just talking. And then she couldn't put on her seatbelt, so I'm helping her with her seatbelt. And so she says to me at that point, can I ask you for a favor? And I said, sure. And she said, can I hold your hand? And I thought it was a bit awkward, but I said, OK, sure. So I'm sitting in the window seat. She was sitting to my left. So I gave her my left hand. And she held on really, really tight with her right hand.

segments.speaker: Tobin Low
segments.text: And this is before the plane has even taken off?

segments.speaker: Leticia Lima
segments.text: Yes. We're starting to taxi very slowly towards the runway. She had her rosary in her left hand, and she's holding my hand. And she had her eyes closed. And she was praying under her breath. I could hear her praying under her-- and it was like, Our Father. And then as the plane starts picking up speed and we're going down the runway, she just switches to saying, like, oh my god. Oh my god. Oh my god. And then as the wheels lift from the runway, you know you get that feeling a little bit in your stomach?

segments.speaker: Tobin Low
segments.text: Uh-huh.

segments.speaker: Leticia Lima
segments.text: And she just turns around and bites me really hard in the forearm.

segments.speaker: Tobin Low
segments.text: Wait. She bites you?

segments.speaker: Leticia Lima
segments.text: Yeah. She lifted the hand that was holding my hand and bit into my forearm really hard.

segments.speaker: Tobin Low
segments.text: Where did she bite you?

segments.speaker: Leticia Lima
segments.text: Close to my elbow, kind of.

segments.speaker: Tobin Low
segments.text: Oh, so like a meaty part of the arm.

segments.speaker: Leticia Lima
segments.text: Yeah, yeah. And she didn't let go for a bit, so I was yelling. And she kind of had her teeth in me.

segments.speaker: Tobin Low
segments.text: How hard did she bite you, would you say?

segments.speaker: Leticia Lima
segments.text: So she did not break my skin. There was no blood.

segments.speaker: Tobin Low
segments.text: Well, that's good. Would you say it was as hard as maybe you would need to bite into a soft piece of bread?

segments.speaker: Leticia Lima
segments.text: More like an apple, I think.

segments.speaker: Tobin Low
segments.text: Oh, so some snap to it.

segments.speaker: Leticia Lima
segments.text: Yeah. And it was quite sudden as well.

segments.speaker: Tobin Low
segments.text: What do you do when she bites onto you?

segments.speaker: Leticia Lima
segments.text: I let out this really loud shout, like a yelp.

segments.speaker: Tobin Low
segments.text: Understandable.

segments.speaker: Leticia Lima
segments.text: Not like a sustained yell, but a really loud ow kind of noise, loud enough that the people who are in the row in front of us and behind us and across from us all kind of turn around. I could see their heads turning in my direction to see what happened.

segments.speaker: Leticia Lima
segments.text: One of them had leaned over and seen that she was biting me and sort of shouted out, she's biting her! At which point, this lady let go, stopped biting me, and also let go of my hand and just started immediately apologizing profusely and saying, I don't know why I did that. I'm so sorry. I've never done that before. And I just kept saying, no, it's OK. Don't worry. It's fine. It's all fine. And she just kept going on and on, and that made it worse.

segments.speaker: Leticia Lima
segments.text: And then the seatbelt signs go off, and it makes that plane noise. And a stewardess comes rushing to our seat and was like, what happened? And again, the person who had seen the bite leans over and says, that lady bit that girl. I didn't say anything. And the stewardess was like, is that true? And the lady goes, yes, yes, it's true. I bit her. And I wanted to say, like, no, nothing happened.

segments.speaker: Tobin Low
segments.text: Oh, no.

segments.speaker: Leticia Lima
segments.text: But the woman was confessing. She was like, no, I did it, and I don't know why I did it. And I'm so sorry I did it. I've never done that before. I felt embarrassed, in a way. And I don't like attention. I'm a fairly introverted person. So it was making me very uncomfortable. I just wanted to listen to my music and put on my sleeping mask and ignore all of this.

segments.speaker: Leticia Lima
segments.text: The stewardess then says to me, can I speak to you privately? Sort of in the back of the airplane, in the galley where they keep their drinks and stuff. So I followed her back there. And she was like, look, do you want to report this incident? Because you have been sort of physically assaulted.

segments.speaker: Tobin Low
segments.text: Oh my god.

segments.speaker: Leticia Lima
segments.text: So you do have the option, if we want. We can call the captain, and he will turn the plane around. And I just said to her, no, absolutely not. Don't worry. Everything is fine. But if you have another empty seat, maybe I could move?

segments.speaker: Tobin Low
segments.text: Oh. They had to have done that for you, right? They must have moved your seat?

segments.speaker: Leticia Lima
segments.text: No. She was like, oh, the flight is fully booked.

segments.speaker: Tobin Low
segments.text: No.

segments.speaker: Leticia Lima
segments.text: And because I think I was a teenager as well, I just said, OK. I didn't argue the point. So then I just went back to my seat.

segments.speaker: Tobin Low
segments.text: Can you remind me, how long is this flight again?

segments.speaker: Leticia Lima
segments.text: It's about 12 hours. And this all happened within the first few minutes of the flight.

segments.speaker: Tobin Low
segments.text: That's so long.

segments.speaker: Leticia Lima
segments.text: It was a very long flight.

segments.speaker: Tobin Low
segments.text: So you're trapped next to her, basically. Like, you're stuck next to this woman who's bit you. What did that feel like?

segments.speaker: Leticia Lima
segments.text: It was clear to me that she felt terrible and that she was still frightened. She did not sleep a wink on that flight. And neither did I. I could tell that she felt really bad. She was still praying and just sort of mumbling to herself quite a bit. Oh, this poor woman. She kind of coiled in on herself.

segments.speaker: Leticia Lima
segments.text: And once I turned my back a little sideways, she did the same, sort of facing out into the aisle. So it was clear to me that she would not want more physical contact, or at least I felt that way. She didn't seem like a threat.

segments.speaker: Tobin Low
segments.text: Did you make any conversation after that point?

segments.speaker: Leticia Lima
segments.text: No, absolute silence the whole way.

segments.speaker: Tobin Low
segments.text: Were you tempted at all to say something?

segments.speaker: Leticia Lima
segments.text: No. I couldn't think of what I would say.

segments.speaker: Tobin Low
segments.text: As you were approaching landing, were you thinking that there might be an interaction moment or you might say something to each other?

segments.speaker: Leticia Lima
segments.text: I thought she would apologize again. I really did. I thought that when she stood up, she would say, oh, and again, I'm so sorry. So I had my whole little "don't worry about it" spiel ready. But she really didn't. She just-- she took her time trying to get all her things back in her purse, and then she got up and left.

segments.speaker: Leticia Lima
segments.text: I got to boarding school. I had this really cool story to tell that no one else would have had. But the more I told it, the more uncomfortable I got. Because a lot of people's reactions were like, yeah, what a crazy woman. And what was she thinking? And I started kind of feeling bad for her. I kept thinking, what would it take for me to feel that scared that I would actually bite someone? And I had, at that point, never been that scared in my life.

segments.speaker: Tobin Low
segments.text: I mean, how do you think about her now?

segments.speaker: Leticia Lima
segments.text: There's a kind of almost, like, fondness there.

segments.speaker: Tobin Low
segments.text: Isn't that funny how sometimes, when you get stuck in a situation with someone, especially something that's hard or long, that stuckness makes you feel like you're comrades, almost, or like you were--

segments.speaker: Leticia Lima
